prompt.context: Our client, Dark Sky, is a small manufacturer of unmanned (i.e. remotely piloted) data collection aircraft. Dark Sky produces the Assessor, an aircraft originally designed for unmanned weather exploration. In 2003, the United States military began purchasing Assessors for use in Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR) missions. The Assessor is profitable, but sales have stagnated and the client wishes to grow.
prompt.question: What are some steps Dark Sky could take to achieve growth?

clarifying_info.q: What does the Assessor do / how does it work?
clarifying_info.a: Dark Sky designs a unique aircraft that is launched from a catapult device; the aircraft can be launched from ships at sea or from harsh terrain (e.g. desert, mountains).

clarifying_info.q: Does Dark Sky sell any other products?
clarifying_info.a: Dark Sky only sells the Assessor, but has designed prototypes specifically for military operations.

There are approximately 20 competitors that manufacture unmanned aircraft. Though too small to purchase a competitor, Dark Sky has been considered an acquisition target. Dark Sky's lack of growth in recent years concerns potential buyers.
Dark Sky's only customer is the U.S. Military.

Dark Sky has a Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee contract with the U.S. Military for Assessor sales. The contract has been extended in the past and is up for renegotiation; the Military has agreed to a marginal fee (i.e. price) increase to account for inflation. Contracts for new aircraft will be structured similarly.

clarifying_info.q: Does Dark Sky have capacity to expand?
clarifying_info.a: The firm has additional capacity and is positioned to strengthen any division of the workforce, if required (e.g. sales force, manufacturing, R&D).

exhibits.title: Dark Sky Revenue 2000–2010
exhibits.shows: A line chart of Dark Sky revenue (in $ millions) from approximately 2000 to 2010
exhibits.data: Y-axis: Revenue ($, Million), scale 0–5; X-axis: years 2000, 2002, 2004, 2006, 2008, 2010; revenue appears near $0.5M in 2002 and peaks near $5M around 2006–2010

exhibits.title: New Product Sales Forecast, 2011
exhibits.shows: A table showing three new aircraft prototypes with their projected Navy and Army unit sales, Assessor cannibalization rates, and per-unit prices
exhibits.data: SeaBird: Navy 50 units, Army 0 units, Assessor cannibalization 40%, price $220,000; SandBird: Navy 0 units, Army 60 units, Assessor cannibalization 70%, price $210,000; JointBird: Navy 38 units, Army 52 units, Assessor cannibalization 90%, price $180,000; Assessor price $110,000

framework: Organic growth – internal levers: (1) increase market penetration with existing Assessor (negotiate more military sales), (2) product development (new aircraft models, training services, accessories/add-ons), (3) new market entry (international markets, Border Patrol, police, news channels), (4) diversification (new product for a new market), (5) pricing adjustments based on demand elasticity

External growth – (1) joint venture with a partner to expand market access or co-develop a product beyond Dark Sky's current capability, (2) merger/acquisition to add capacity or product mix; given Dark Sky's small size, also consider becoming an acquisition target to unlock value

questions.prompt: Exhibit 1a: How many units were sold in 2010?
questions.guidance: Read 2010 revenue from the chart (~$5,000k) and divide by price per unit ($100k). Answer: 50 units.

questions.prompt: Exhibit 1b: What was the revenue growth rate from 2002 to 2006?
questions.guidance: Read 2002 revenue (~$500k) and 2006 revenue (~$5,000k) from the chart, then calculate percentage growth. Answer: 900%.

questions.prompt: Exhibit 2: To maximize short-term (2011) revenue, which new aircraft should Dark Sky introduce — SeaBird, SandBird, or JointBird?
questions.guidance: For each option calculate total 2011 revenue = Assessor revenue (post-cannibalization) + new product revenue. The Military has agreed to raise the Assessor price to $110,000. Baseline without any new product: 50 Assessors × $110,000 = $5,500,000. Introducing a new aircraft cannibalizes some Assessor sales per Exhibit 2. Compare all three totals; JointBird yields the highest revenue at $16,750,000.

math.setup: Total revenue = (Assessor units remaining × $110,000) + (new product units × new product price)
math.answer: JointBird yields the highest 2011 total revenue: $16,750,000 vs. $14,300,000 (SeaBird) and $14,250,000 (SandBird)

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond the immediate revenue calculation, what additional factors should Dark Sky consider before committing to JointBird production?

categories.name: Production sequencing
ideas: How quickly could Dark Sky start manufacturing a third model — could it produce SandBird this year and add SeaBird the following year?
What are the revenue implications of a phased multi-model rollout versus launching only JointBird?

categories.name: Profitability and cost allocation
ideas: How profitable are the four aircraft models relative to one another?
Because Dark Sky has a Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee contract, profitability per aircraft is likely equivalent — so focus should be on maximizing units sold
With JointBird, is the remaining $550,000 in Assessor revenue worth the associated production cost, or should those resources be redeployed?

categories.name: Investment and payback
ideas: How much capital investment is required to manufacture each new aircraft type?
What is the payback period for each option?

categories.name: Long-term revenue and strategic fit
ideas: Does the short-term revenue advantage of JointBird hold over a multi-year horizon?
What are the risks of near-total Assessor cannibalization (90%) if JointBird underperforms?
Competitive response — how might the 20 existing competitors react to Dark Sky's new product launch?
Could introducing a dual-service aircraft attract additional government customers or facilitate an acquisition at a higher valuation?

recommendation: Based on 2011 forecasted revenue, Dark Sky should introduce the JointBird to the U.S. Military — it generates $16,750,000 in total revenue, outperforming SeaBird ($14,300,000) and SandBird ($14,250,000) and nearly tripling the Assessor-only baseline ($5,500,000)
JointBird serves both Navy and Army, providing the broadest market coverage and the highest unit volume (90 new aircraft)
risks: JointBird cannibalizes 90% of Assessor sales, reducing Assessor units from 50 to just 5 — near-total dependency on the new platform
As a compromise aircraft, JointBird may be less operationally effective than SeaBird or SandBird for their respective missions, risking lower repeat orders
Significant upfront investment required; payback period and profitability details need to be confirmed
Competitive response from the ~20 rival manufacturers could erode pricing or unit-sales assumptions
Dark Sky's lack of recent growth has already flagged it as an underperforming acquisition target — execution risk of a new product launch is real
next_steps: Confirm cost structure and profitability under the Cost-Plus-Fixed-Fee contract for each aircraft model
Model multi-year revenue scenarios including the possibility of eventually producing multiple new aircraft
Assess manufacturing timeline and capital requirements for JointBird production
Evaluate whether keeping Assessor production at 5 units is economically viable or whether resources should be fully redirected
Conduct a strategic review of M&A / JV options that could accelerate production capacity or expand the customer base beyond the U.S. Military
